transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-29
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Evan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (BlueMesa CTO), Priya Patel (Infra Lead), Sam Carter (SWE), Elena Gonzalez (Data Scientist)

Summary: exploratory integration discovery; BlueMesa evaluates Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private for customer-facing summarization API. Focus areas: SDK support (python/node), LangChain / LlamaIndex connectors, gateway/proxy patterns (sidecar vs centralized), rate limits/quotas and token accounting, and observability hooks for latency/cost per request.

Links referenced: Redwood quickstart (short link: rwd.co/quickstart), LangChain adapter draft (rwd.co/langchain-adpt), internal perf spreadsheet (shared via drive link)

--- Transcript ---
[00:00:03] Evan: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Evan from Redwood, AE. With me is Maya, our SE who will run through architecture. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:11] Jordan: Good, thanks. Busy week but excited to chat.
[00:00:13] Priya: Hi all. Priya here, infra. We're mainly worried about egress and data residency.
[00:00:18] Maya: Great, we'll cover those. Quick agenda: you said you want to support a public summarization endpoint for enterprise customers, is that right?
[00:00:26] Jordan: Correct, it's a multi-tenant API where customers send docs and we return structured summaries. Latency target 300-500ms p50 for short docs, and throughput of 400 concurrent rps in peak. Cost is a factor.
[00:00:36] Sam: Also want to plug into existing LangChain pipelines and LlamaIndex loaders; we're heavy on Python.
[00:00:41] Evan: Makes sense. At a high level Redwood can run as hosted API (fast onboarding), Dedicated (reserved GPU pools), or Private (VPC/on-prem). We typically see teams start hosted for proof of concept then move to Dedicated or Private for compliance.
[00:00:52] Jordan: Two immediate questions: can we run the same code path if we switch from hosted to dedicated? And how do SDKs look?
[00:00:59] Maya: Yes, API and SDKs are consistent. Our Python and Node SDKs are identical surface area. We have LangChain connectors and a LlamaIndex integration — we call it the "index adapter" in the docs. Quick note the adapter is experimental for some model variants.
[00:01:12] [00:01:15] Priya: When you say LangChain connectors, we mean we can swap provider in our pipelines transparently?
[00:01:20] Maya: Yep. For LangChain you can set the provider to Redwood and pass the same chains. We also provide a small proxy pattern sample that shows a gateway sitting in front of the Redwood endpoint to handle auth and quota at our side.
[00:01:32] Jordan: Can you say more about that gateway/proxy sample? We're looking at either a sidecar per service or a central gateway. Which do you recommend?
[00:01:40] Maya: It depends. Sidecar gives microsecond-level network overhead but complicates deployments; central gateway simplifies auth and rate-limiting. Our sample shows both: a lightweight edge proxy (we've seen teams use Envoy) and a central token-bucket gateway pattern.
[00:01:54] Sam: Are there examples for integrating with our existing API gateway (Kong)?
[00:01:58] Evan: We have a Kong plugin example — will share. It shows token accounting and route-level quotas.
[00:02:03] [00:02:10] Jordan: Observability is key. We need per-request latency and per-token cost tagging in our traces. How mature are your hooks?
[00:02:18] Maya: We expose per-request headers and response metadata — model id, tokens_in/out, cost_estimate, and a request id you can map to trace. We also have a tracing shim for OpenTelemetry and sample dashboards in Redwood Console for token/cost breakdown.
[00:02:32] Priya: Is the token accounting done server-side or do we need to compute tokens in our app?
[00:02:36] Maya: Redwood returns token counts. We also provide an SDK helper that does client-side estimation for pre-request cost checks. But authoritative billing token counts come from Redwood.
[00:02:44] [00:02:50] Sam: About rate limits: at peak we might route 400 rps but with bursts up to 1200 rps for short windows; can Redwood absorb that with hosted?
[00:02:58] Evan: Hosted has auto-scaling and burst, but sustained 400 rps with consistent low tail latency we recommend Dedicated. You can use hosted for bursts during early stages. Dedicated gives predictable throughput and options to configure autoscale policies and burst cushions.
[00:03:11] Jordan: If we move to Dedicated, how does model rollouts and version pinning work? We can't have silent regressions.
[00:03:18] Maya: Dedicated lets you pin model versions per route, canary rollouts and automatic fallback policies. We also integrate with our Optimize service that suggests quantization and batch sizes for your workload and flags quality regressions against your prompt set.
[00:03:31] [00:03:40] Priya: For Private deployment — VPC or on-prem — can the control plane be managed by Redwood and data paths stay inside our VPC?
[00:03:47] Maya: Yes, Private supports a customer-managed VPC peering model where inference nodes live in your VPC and the control plane handles metadata; or fully air-gapped on-prem packages. Network egress is configurable; we support KMS integration for keys.
[00:03:59] Jordan: Our security team will ask about SOC2 and audit logs and RBAC.
[00:04:03] Evan: We have SOC 2 Type II and SAML SSO + fine-grained RBAC. Audit logs are available in the Console and via streaming to your SIEM. We'll attach the security whitepaper.
[00:04:12] [00:04:20] Sam: Small thing — LlamaIndex loader support; some of our docs are large. How does Redwood handle long context? Do you have prefix caching / kv cache features?
[00:04:29] Maya: Our runtime supports KV cache and prefix caching techniques to reduce repeated compute for long contexts, also continuous batching. For very long docs we usually recommend chunking + retrieval with an embedding store. We also provide suggestions for quantization profiles to cut cost.
[00:04:44] Priya: Do you have benchmarks for p50/p95 at different sequence lengths?
[00:04:48] Maya: Yes — we have a perf spreadsheet. Quick summary: on Dedicated with A100-style instances and optimized kernels, p50 for 512-token is sub-200ms, p95 around 350ms in our test harness. We'll share the spreadsheet but note results vary by model and load.
[00:05:03] [00:05:15] Jordan: About pricing: we need hosted per-token pricing and Dedicated committed capacity pricing. Any ballpark?
[00:05:22] Evan: I'll send a pricing matrix. Hosted is usage-based per-token plus egress; Dedicated is monthly committed slots with a lower unit cost and options for burst. The spreadsheet we'll send will show sample TCO for 6/12 month commitments.
[00:05:33] Sam: For our stacks we run everything in Python. The SDKs — do they support async calls and streaming?
[00:05:39] Maya: Yes — Python async/await and Node streams are supported. Streaming responses include incremental tokens and chunked metadata. The LangChain connector supports streaming chain-of-thought style generators.
[00:05:51] [00:06:05] Priya: Network security: if we use hosted, how do we lock access down so only our services call the endpoints?
[00:06:10] Evan: You can use API keys + IP allowlists and per-route JWT-based auth. For Dedicated/Private we provide VPC peering and can limit egress.
[00:06:20] Jordan: We also need to know about data retention — can inbound customer payloads be disabled from being stored?
[00:06:26] Maya: Yes. We have data retention policies per-account. For regulated customers you can set zero retention and opt out of logging. For Dedicated/Private you can also choose to not send usage events to Redwood control plane.
[00:06:36] [00:06:50] Sam: One architectural question: we currently have a per-tenant microservice that calls models for summaries synchronously. Would you recommend a synchronous call to Redwood or an async job queue with worker pools?
[00:06:58] Maya: If latency SLO is tight (<=500ms p50) and payloads are small, synchronous calls to a dedicated pool are fine. If you have heavy pre/post-processing or large documents, async with worker pools helps control concurrency and retry. A common pattern: gateway receives requests, does quick validation, computes embeddings if needed, then fanout to worker pool calling Redwood with pinned model routes.
[00:07:15] Jordan: Any gotchas integrating LlamaIndex? We've seen memory issues with big indexes.
[00:07:20] Maya: For LlamaIndex we recommend streaming writes to the embedding store and checkpointing. Our LlamaIndex adapter supports chunked ingestion and backpressure. Also watch KV cache size — our docs show how to TTL the cache.
[00:07:33] [00:07:45] Priya: How about SLOs on tail latency when batch sizes increase?
[00:07:49] Maya: Batching improves throughput but can increase tail latency. Our Optimize tool recommends batch sizes based on your latency SLOs and the model's sequence length distribution. You can configure max-batch-delay to cap latency.
[00:08:02] Sam: Are there quotas per API key? We want per-customer quotas to enforce tiers.
[00:08:06] Evan: Yes. You can set per-api-key quotas, route-level quotas, and org-level caps. Quotas can be enforced at gateway or by Redwood if you use our token-based system.
[00:08:17] Jordan: On the observability side, can we get traces wired into our existing Datadog?
[00:08:21] Maya: We provide OpenTelemetry spans and metrics that you can send to Datadog. Also exportable logs for SIEM ingestion.
[00:08:29] [00:08:40] Priya: For Private deployment, how long does an on-prem install take? Weeks? Months?
[00:08:45] Evan: Typical Private VPC onboarding is 2-4 weeks depending on networking approvals. Fully air-gapped on-prem can be 6-12 weeks due to procurement and security reviews. We have a deployment checklist that speeds this up.
[00:08:57] Sam: Any examples of customers who've moved from hosted to Dedicated successfully?
[00:09:01] Evan: Yes, a few — we'll anonymize case studies. Key lessons: start with hosted to validate prompts, add observability hooks early, then plan Dedicated right before large scale commitments.
[00:09:10] [00:09:25] Jordan: Security question: KMS — do you support customer-managed keys?
[00:09:29] Maya: We integrate with major KMS providers (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure KeyVault) and support HSM for Private installs.
[00:09:36] Priya: For billing, can we get token-level export daily?
[00:09:41] Evan: Yes, usage exports are available as CSV or streamed to your billing pipeline.
[00:09:47] [00:09:55] Jordan: Let's talk about a small pilot. Hypothetical: 50 rps sustained, 500 concurrent users, average payload 120 tokens in, 200 out. What would you recommend for the pilot footprint?
[00:10:07] Maya: For that profile hosted could work for a short pilot; Dedicated with 2-3 reserved slots would give predictable latency for a longer pilot and smoother billing. We can run benchmarks with your sample requests and share p50/p95 numbers.
[00:10:19] Sam: Can we test with our LangChain pipelines in a POC?
[00:10:22] Evan: Absolutely. SE can provide a LangChain quickstart and a LlamaIndex loader example to run with your data.
[00:10:28] [00:10:35] Maya: I'll also provide a proxy sample for Kong and Envoy plus an OpenTelemetry config. That will show per-request token metrics and how to attribute cost.
[00:10:46] Priya: Network diagram: we need to know if egress is to Redwood control plane IP ranges or if everything stays inside VPC for Private.
[00:10:53] Maya: For hosted, egress goes to Redwood's public endpoints (we'll provide IP ranges and NAT guidance). For Private, inference nodes are inside your VPC — control plane communication is optional and can be restricted.
[00:11:05] [00:11:20] Jordan: Timeline — we'd like to have a POC within 3 weeks to show to execs. Is that feasible?
[00:11:27] Evan: Yes. Typical POC timeline: day 0-3 get API keys and quickstart, day 4-10 run integration and run sample benchmarks, day 11-21 evaluate results and iterate. We'll staff a short SE engagement for the POC.
[00:11:38] Sam: Any specific rate-limiting behavior we should watch for when using streaming responses?
[00:11:42] Maya: Streaming is backpressure-aware — if a client is slow we have configurable circuit breakers. Rate limits apply per interactive session and per API key; our SDK exposes hooks to surface 429s and retry-after headers.
[00:11:56] [00:12:10] Priya: For multi-tenant billing attribution, do you provide per-tenant token reporting?
[00:12:14] Maya: You can either use separate API keys per tenant and pull usage per key, or route tenant metadata in headers and use our token attribution features to split costs per tenant.
[00:12:25] Jordan: That header approach might be simpler.
[00:12:30] Evan: We'll include an example.
[00:12:34] [00:12:50] (Brief cross-talk about time zones and scheduling)
[00:12:55] Maya: Quick demo? I can show a LangChain sample invoking Redwood and the Console token dashboard.
[00:13:01] Jordan: Yes, please.
[00:13:02] [screen share demo — audio summary captured]
[00:13:05] Maya: (walkthrough) Here's the Python snippet: from redwood import Client; client = Client(api_key='REDACTED'); response = client.generate(...). This will stream tokens and the response metadata includes token counts. On the Console you can see per-route token breakdown.
[00:13:23] Elena: That looks straightforward.
[00:13:25] Maya: Now switching to the LangChain adapter — you wire Redwood as the llm provider and the chain is unchanged. The adapter supports streaming callbacks for async Chains.
[00:13:35] Sam: Any gotchas migrating from OpenAI SDK call shapes?
[00:13:39] Maya: We try to be compatible, but parameter names differ slightly — we'll provide a migration guide. Our SDK also includes a thin compatibility layer for common OpenAI params.
[00:13:49] [00:14:05] Jordan: Let's talk about a few constraints: 1) We need SSO integration for our internal team to manage keys. 2) Security wants audit exports. 3) Legal will ask about subprocessors — any list?
[00:14:15] Evan: For SSO we support SAML and OIDC. Audit exports are supported. We'll include a standard subprocessors list in the security pack.
[00:14:28] Priya: If we go Dedicated, how does scaling work for unexpected traffic spikes?
[00:14:33] Maya: Dedicated can be configured with burst capacity: you reserve base slots and allow short-term burst consumption billed at an overage rate. There's also routing policy to fallback to hosted in case Dedicated is exhausted — but that's optional based on your risk tolerance.
[00:14:46] Sam: So fallback could be another model variant smaller or hosted region?
[00:14:50] Maya: Exactly — model variants or cheaper quantized variants as fallback.
[00:14:55] [00:15:10] Jordan: For compliance, any certifications beyond SOC 2?
[00:15:14] Evan: We have SOC 2 Type II; ISO 27001 is underway. We can put you in touch with our compliance team for an NDA'd questionnaire.
[00:15:24] Priya: We need to run an internal benchmark. Can Redwood run the benchmarks with our sample dataset?
[00:15:30] Maya: Yes, we can run benchmarks in our test harness using your curl/sample client. We'll need sample payloads and expected concurrency.
[00:15:38] Jordan: I'll get that over.
[00:15:40] [00:15:55] (brief pause)
[00:16:00] Evan: Recap and next steps: Evan to send pricing matrix and case studies; Maya to share LangChain/LlamaIndex quickstart, Kong/Envoy proxy samples, OpenTelemetry config, and the perf spreadsheet. BlueMesa to share sample request logs and network diagram. SE engagement kick-off call to schedule next week. Does that sound right?
[00:16:18] Jordan: Yes. Also add security docs to the shared drop.
[00:16:21] Evan: Will do.
[00:16:23] Priya: One more ask — can we get a nightly export of token usage during the POC?
[00:16:28] Maya: Yes we can enable daily usage exports and a dashboard.
[00:16:31] Jordan: Great. Timeline: we'll aim to start POC next Monday.
[00:16:35] Evan: Perfect — we'll follow up with calendar invites and an SE kickoff.
[00:16:38] (meeting winds down; small talk)
[00:16:50] End of recording.
